Assuming the population you're studying is very large, it is 1.96*sqrt((p*(1-p))/n) where p is the proportion of the result you're looking at, n is the sample size and 1.96 is the number of standard deviations from the mean for 95% confidence, ie the distance you have to go out from the center of the normal distribution to hit the 2.5% tails (this number would be different if you were looking for the error rate at a different confidence level). Note something that people often don't realize and that is that p(1-p) is a maximum for p=0.5 (0.25), so the error a result is subject to is a maximum when the result you're measuring is 50%... the closer you move to measuring something closer to 0% or 100%, the smaller your error band gets. So strictly speaking, the error rate quoted for a survey is a maximum MOE, me and different results in the same survey have different errors. Alternatively, do it the easy way and plug your numbers into any number of online margin of error calculators. ;-)

CPI is not exactly a measure of "inflation"or at the very least it is not the only measure of inflation, but it is what the Bank of Canada means when they say "inflation". In Canada real estate is calculated two ways: Mortgage payment costs and a measure of 'depreciation' of housing. The reasoning is that Canadians, with extremely few exceptions, don't buy houses outright but instead take out a mortgage on that house and that mortgage is what they are paying. Other countries use different ow measures for real estate while several countries don't include real estate costs at all in their CPI calculation deeming that it is an asset/investment rather than a good or service purchased by consumers (same reasoning as to why stock prices aren't included in CPI).
